claim: Dietary restriction extends healthy lifespan across a broad range of taxa, from yeast to primates.
source: Dietary restriction, also called calorie restriction, is a moderate reduction in food intake that extends healthy lifespan across a broad range of taxa, ﻿from yeast to primates (Chapman and Partridge, 1996; Colman et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2002; McCay et al., 1935).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research

claim: The disposable soma theory postulates that organisms will maximise fitness by strategically partitioning limiting dietary energy either to reproduction or somatic maintenance.
source: This theory postulates that organisms will maximise fitness by strategically partitioning limiting dietary energy either to reproduction or somatic maintenance, the latter determining lifespan.
evidence: Refers to established theoretical framework with citations

claim: High protein, low carbohydrate diets are consistently associated with high reproduction and short lifespan.
source: Specifically, high protein, low carbohydrate diets are consistently associated with high reproduction and short lifespan, while low-protein, high-carbohydrate diets are associated with longer lifespan and lower levels of reproduction (Piper et al., 2011; Simpson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Low-protein, high-carbohydrate diets are associated with longer lifespan and lower levels of reproduction.
source: Specifically, high protein, low carbohydrate diets are consistently associated with high reproduction and short lifespan, while low-protein, high-carbohydrate diets are associated with longer lifespan and lower levels of reproduction (Piper et al., 2011; Simpson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: The effect of protein dilution on lifespan is mediated by reducing signalling through the amino acid sensitive Target Of Rapamycin (TOR) pathway to enhance cellular proteostasis.
source: Accumulating evidence indicates that the effect is mediated by reducing signalling through the amino acid sensitive Target Of Rapamycin (TOR) pathway to enhance cellular proteostasis (Sanz et al., 2004; Ayala et al., 2007; Raubenheimer and Simpson, 2009; Simpson and Raubenheimer, 2009; Taylor and Dillin, 2011; Fanson et al., 2012; Sabatini, 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research

claim: Dietary protein is the principle driver of egg production in Drosophila melanogaster females.
source: Although protein is key, females must transfer dozens of nutrients into eggs for future embryo formation and not all of these components contribute to the flies' decision to produce eggs (Piper et al., 2014; Mirth et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations and logical inference from the text

claim: Depriving adult female flies of dietary sterols imposes a minor cost on reproduction but a substantial (>50%) cost to lifespan.
source: We have previously found that depriving adult female flies of a source of sterols, an essential micronutrient for insects, imposes a minor cost on reproduction, but a substantial (>50%) cost to lifespan (Piper et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research by the authors

claim: Egg production showed a linear, positive correlation with dietary protein content.
source: Specifically, egg production showed a linear, positive correlation with dietary protein content (Figure 1, Supplementary file 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and statistical analysis

claim: Lifespan showed a peak at intermediate protein (66 d median at 10.7 g/l), and fell away at both higher (49 d median at 33.1 g/l) and lower (43 d median at 5.2 g/l) concentrations.
source: while lifespan showed a peak at intermediate protein (66 d median at 10.7 g/l), and fell away at both higher (49 d median at 33.1 g/l) and lower (43 d median at 5.2 g/l) concentrations (Figure 1a–b, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and statistical analysis

claim: Restricting dietary protein from high to intermediate levels increased lifespan and decreased reproduction.
source: Thus, as is typical for dietary restriction experiments, restricting dietary protein from high to intermediate levels increased lifespan and decreased reproduction (Lee et al., 2008; Skorupa et al., 2008; Grandison et al., 2009; Katewa et al., 2016; Le Couteur et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to published research

claim: Egg laying was suppressed in a dose-dependent fashion by increasing dietary carbohydrate.
source: When increasing dietary carbohydrate against an otherwise fixed nutritional background, egg laying was suppressed in a dose-dependent fashion, but lifespan remained at its maximum level and was unchanged across all carbohydrate doses (~66 d median, Figure 1c–d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1

claim: Lifespan remained at its maximum level and was unchanged across all carbohydrate doses when increasing dietary carbohydrate.
source: When increasing dietary carbohydrate against an otherwise fixed nutritional background, egg laying was suppressed in a dose-dependent fashion, but lifespan remained at its maximum level and was unchanged across all carbohydrate doses (~66 d median, Figure 1c–d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1

claim: The diet with the lowest concentration of carbohydrate (5.7 g/l) and intermediate protein level (10.7 g/l) supported both maximum lifespan (66 d median) and the highest level of egg laying (75 eggs/female).
source: The diet with the lowest concentration of carbohydrate (5.7 g/l), which also contained the intermediate protein level (10.7 g/l), supported both maximum lifespan (Figure 1d; 66 d median) and the highest level of egg laying (75 eggs/female) of any diet in our experiment.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1

claim: Balancing the dietary protein and carbohydrate concentrations can reveal a single dietary optimum for both lifespan and reproduction.
source: Thus, as we have previously shown (Piper et al., 2017), balancing the dietary protein and carbohydrate concentrations can reveal a single dietary optimum for both traits, showing that lifespan shortening is not necessarily caused by high egg laying alone.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to previous work

claim: Diet type (defined by variation of macronutrient composition) and variation in cholesterol concentration both significantly modified egg laying and lifespan.
source: Initial analysis of the data showed that diet type, when defined by variation of macronutrient composition, as well as variation in cholesterol concentration both significantly modified egg laying and lifespan (Figure 2, Supplementary files 3 and 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and statistical analysis

claim: There was no main effect of dietary energy density (calories) on egg laying or lifespan.
source: By contrast, we saw no main effect of dietary energy density (calories) on either trait, which is consistent with previous findings showing that these traits are driven by the relative proportion of protein and carbohydrate in the diet independently of caloric value (Lee et al., 2008; Mair et al., 2005; Skorupa et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to published research

claim: Lowering dietary cholesterol was detrimental for lifespan and intensified the negative effects of increasing dietary protein concentrations.
source: Thus, lowering dietary cholesterol was detrimental for lifespan and it intensified the negative effects of increasing dietary protein concentrations.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: Increasing cholesterol from 0 g/l to 0.15 g/l amplified the positive effect on egg laying of increasing dietary protein.
source: Increasing cholesterol from 0 g/l (Figure 2a) to 0.15 g/l (Figure 2c) amplified the positive effect on egg laying of increasing dietary protein.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: The response of egg laying to increasing protein was only compromised when cholesterol was completely removed from the diet, or when cholesterol was low (0.15 g/l) and protein was high (30 g/l).
source: Thus, the response of egg laying to increasing protein was only compromised when cholesterol was completely removed from the diet, or when cholesterol was low (0.15 g/l) and protein was high (30 g/l) (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: At 0 g/l cholesterol, lifespan was generally short (31d median) but positively affected by increasing dietary carbohydrate (up to 40 d median).
source: At 0 g/l cholesterol, lifespan was generally short (31d median) but positively affected by increasing dietary carbohydrate (up to 40 d median) (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: When cholesterol reached 0.3 g/l, the flies were constantly long-lived, and lifespan was unaffected by dietary carbohydrate level (66 d median).
source: However, when cholesterol reached 0.3 g/l, the flies were constantly long-lived, and lifespan was unaffected by dietary carbohydrate level (66 d median) (Figure 2f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: Each dietary carbohydrate level could support maximal fly lifespan, but the lower carbohydrate diets were more susceptible to the detrimental effects of dietary cholesterol dilution.
source: Thus, each of our dietary carbohydrate levels could support maximal fly lifespan, but the lower carbohydrate diets were more susceptible to the detrimental effects of dietary cholesterol dilution.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: Increasing cholesterol benefited egg laying more at lower dietary carbohydrate levels.
source: This increasingly negative relationship between carbohydrate and egg laying was caused because increasing cholesterol benefited egg laying more at lower dietary carbohydrate levels – the opposite of what we observed for lifespan.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: The benefits of cholesterol addition were not related to the caloric content of the diet.
source: We also found that the benefits of cholesterol addition were not related to the caloric content of the diet because cholesterol improved fecundity and extended lifespan of flies on almost all diets, including those with the lowest, intermediate, and highest caloric densities (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Lowering cholesterol produces worse outcomes as the dietary protein: carbohydrate ratio increases.
source: Instead, lowering cholesterol produces worse outcomes as the dietary protein: carbohydrate ratio increases.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data

claim: Flies produce more eggs in response to increasing dietary protein: carbohydrate ratio and these positive effects persist even as dietary cholesterol falls to a level that cannot fully support lifespan (less than 0.3 g/l cholesterol).
source: We saw that flies produce more eggs in response to increasing dietary protein: carbohydrate ratio and that these positive effects persist even as dietary cholesterol falls to a level that cannot fully support lifespan (less than 0.3 g/l cholesterol).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data

claim: There is a positive relationship between the dietary protein: carbohydrate ratio and egg laying across all levels of dietary cholesterol.
source: This is indeed what we found, although the positive relationship was modified by cholesterol level (Figure 3a,c,e,g, Supplementary file 7), starting with a weak positive effect on 0 g/l cholesterol (Figure 3a) and becoming increasingly positive as cholesterol was increased to 0.15 g/l (Figure 3c) and 0.3 g/l (Figure 3e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: When cholesterol was at 0 g/l, there was a negative relationship between egg laying and lifespan.
source: When the data are grouped by dietary cholesterol level (Figure 3), we see that when cholesterol was at 0 g/l (Figure 3b), there was a negative relationship between egg laying and lifespan
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: As cholesterol level increased, the negative correlation between egg laying and lifespan flattened, such that the slope was no longer negative for each level of cholesterol supplementation.
source: but as the cholesterol level increased, the correlation flattened, such that the slope was no longer negative for each level of cholesterol supplementation (Figure 3d,f,h, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and statistical analysis

claim: When dietary cholesterol was insufficient, increasing dietary protein: carbohydrate drove higher egg laying and this predicted lifespan shortening.
source: Thus, when dietary cholesterol was insufficient, increasing dietary protein: carbohydrate drove higher egg laying (Figure 3a) and this predicted lifespan shortening (Figure 3b) – a scenario that exemplifies the negative relationship between reproduction and lifespan in response to increasing protein: carbohydrate levels that is regularly reported in the dietary restriction literature (Mair et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2008; Skorupa et al., 2008; Solon-Biet et al., 2014; Solon-Biet et al., 2015; Simpson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and citations

claim: When cholesterol was increased, egg laying was either completely independent of lifespan or became slightly positively correlated.
source: However, when cholesterol was increased, the negative relationship was reduced such that egg laying was either completely independent of lifespan (Figure 3d) or became slightly positively correlated, indicating that the dietary conditions, which promote egg laying, are the same as those that promote longer lifespan (Figure 3f,h).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: Higher egg laying in response to increasing protein: carbohydrate levels only shortens lifespan when cholesterol is insufficient to support egg production.
source: Thus, higher egg laying in response to increasing protein: carbohydrate levels only shortens lifespan when cholesterol is insufficient to support egg production.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: TOR activity increases with dietary protein levels.
source: Because TOR activity increases with dietary protein levels, it has been implicated as mediating the detrimental effects on lifespan of high protein diets (Liu and Sabatini, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: Rapamycin extends lifespan across numerous species, including Drosophila.
source: This is supported by the fact that rapamycin, a pharmacological suppressor of TOR, has been shown to extend lifespan across numerous species, including Drosophila where it also suppresses egg production across different caloric densities (Bjedov et al., 2010; Schinaman et al., 2019; Scialò et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Rapamycin suppresses egg production in Drosophila across different caloric densities.
source: This is supported by the fact that rapamycin, a pharmacological suppressor of TOR, has been shown to extend lifespan across numerous species, including Drosophila where it also suppresses egg production across different caloric densities (Bjedov et al., 2010; Schinaman et al., 2019; Scialò et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Increasing dietary cholesterol from 0.1 to 0.3 g/l increased lifespan (62 d median v 69 d median) on a high protein: carbohydrate diet.
source: As before, when we maintained flies on a high protein: carbohydrate diet, increasing dietary cholesterol from 0.1 to 0.3 g/l increased lifespan (62 d median v 69 d median)(Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: Egg laying was slightly (34%), but significantly, elevated by cholesterol supplementation from 0.1 to 0.3 g/l on a high protein: carbohydrate diet.
source: Egg laying was also slightly (34%), but significantly, elevated by cholesterol supplementation (Figure 4b) indicating that 0.1 g/l cholesterol was limiting for both lifespan and reproduction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: When rapamycin was added to both foods, egg laying was almost completely suppressed.
source: When rapamycin was added to both foods, egg laying was almost completely suppressed (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: Rapamycin extended fly lifespan, but only for flies on low dietary cholesterol (0.1 g/l).
source: Rapamycin also extended fly lifespan, but only for flies on low dietary cholesterol (0.1 g/l)(Figure 4a), bringing their lifespan up to the same level as flies on higher cholesterol food (0.3 g/l; 69 d median).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: Adding rapamycin to the food with higher cholesterol (0.3 g/l) did not result in any additional lifespan improvement over what was already achieved by increasing cholesterol alone.
source: Adding rapamycin to the food with higher cholesterol did not result in any additional lifespan improvement over what was already achieved by increasing cholesterol alone (69 d median; Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: Lifespan extension by rapamycin administration is conditional on the flies being on a low cholesterol diet.
source: These data show that lifespan extension by rapamycin administration is conditional on the flies being on a low cholesterol diet.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: Adding 0.3 g/l cholesterol to both the low yeast (dietary restriction) and high yeast foods of both yeast types had a significant positive effect on lifespan.
source: Adding 0.3 g/l cholesterol to both the low yeast (dietary restriction) and high yeast foods of both yeast types had a significant positive effect on lifespan (Figure 5a,c)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: Adding 0.3 g/l cholesterol to both the low yeast and high yeast foods of both yeast types had a significant positive effect on egg laying.
source: Adding 0.3 g/l cholesterol to both the low yeast (dietary restriction) and high yeast foods of both yeast types had a significant positive effect on lifespan (Figure 5a,c) and egg laying (Figure 5b,d) when compared to diets without cholesterol supplementation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: The magnitude of the lifespan benefit from cholesterol supplementation was greater for flies on the high yeast foods than on the low yeast foods.
source: The magnitude of this benefit to lifespan was greater for flies on the high yeast foods than on the low yeast foods, meaning that cholesterol supplementation narrowed the difference between the dietary restriction vs high yeast diet from 9 to 4% for flies on the autolysed yeast diets (Figure 5a) and from 81 to 25% lifespan extension for flies on the yeast extract diets (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: Even with cholesterol supplementation, the flies on the high yeast diet were still significantly shorter lived than those on the cholesterol supplemented low yeast food.
source: We note that even with cholesterol supplementation, the flies on the high yeast diet were still significantly shorter lived than those on the cholesterol supplemented low yeast food.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: The role of protein and carbohydrate on lifespan is indirect, acting by altering the partitioning of limiting amounts of dietary sterols between reproduction and lifespan.
source: Using Drosophila melanogaster, we show that the role of protein and carbohydrate on lifespan is indirect, acting by altering the partitioning of limiting amounts of dietary sterols between reproduction and lifespan.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Shorter lifespans in flies fed on high protein: carbohydrate diets can be rescued by supplementing their food with cholesterol.
source: Shorter lifespans in flies fed on high protein: carbohydrate diets can be rescued by supplementing their food with cholesterol.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Diets with high protein: carbohydrate ratios decrease lifespan by causing mothers to overinvest limiting sterols into egg production.
source: Specifically, diets with high protein: carbohydrate ratios decrease lifespan by causing mothers to overinvest limiting sterols into egg production.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and discussion

claim: Non-reproducing adult males and genetically sterile females suffer little to no lifespan cost when sterol deprived.
source: It is also consistent with our recent work that showed non-reproducing adult males and genetically sterile females suffer little to no lifespan cost when sterol deprived, which is presumably because they conserve sterols which would otherwise be depleted by reproduction (Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent work by the authors

claim: Yeast contains all of the nutrients that flies require, including protein (~45%), carbohydrate (~40%), a small amount of fat (~7%), nucleic acids (~7%), and micronutrients, such as sterols, metal ions and vitamins.
source: Yeast contains all of the nutrients that flies require, including protein (~45%), carbohydrate (~40%), a small amount of fat (~7%), nucleic acids (~7%), and micronutrients, such as sterols, metal ions and vitamins, which are essential for flies.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about yeast composition

claim: Drosophila select amongst foods containing the appropriate protein and carbohydrate concentrations to enhance their fitness.
source: Drosophila rely heavily on protein from yeast, as well as carbohydrate from both yeast and plant sources, to guide their feeding behaviour. They select amongst foods containing the appropriate protein and carbohydrate concentrations to enhance their fitness (Ribeiro and Dickson, 2010; Vargas et al., 2010; Walker et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Sterols do not affect Drosophila feeding behaviour.
source: Many of the other nutrients from their diet, including sterols, do not affect feeding behaviour, presumably because they are normally acquired in adequate quantities as part of a diet that is sufficient in macronutrients (Walker et al., 2015; Leitão-Gonçalves et al., 2017; Münch et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: The abundance of sterols in yeast can vary over a 10-fold range in response to changes in oxygen availability.
source: While the proportion of protein and carbohydrate in yeast remains relatively constant across growth conditions, the abundance of sterols can vary over a 10-fold range in response to changes in oxygen availability, which is essential for sterol biosynthesis (Starr and Parks, 1962; Wilson and McLeod, 1976).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Fly lifespan is susceptible to reductions in the sterol: protein content of dietary yeast because protein drives sterols to be preferentially partitioned towards reproduction at the expense of maintaining the adult soma.
source: Thus, because fly feeding behaviour and egg production are almost entirely shaped by the macronutrients, fly lifespan is susceptible to reductions in the sterol: protein content of dietary yeast. Our data indicate that this is because protein drives sterols to be preferentially partitioned towards reproduction at the expense of maintaining the adult soma.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and discussion

claim: The trade-off between reproduction and lifespan can exist for flies feeding on yeast, but only when dietary sterols are limiting.
source: Our data indicate that this trade-off can exist for flies feeding on yeast, but only when dietary sterols are limiting.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and discussion

claim: When dietary sterols are not limiting, the trade-off between reproduction and lifespan does not need to exist and a single nutritional optimum for both lifespan and reproduction can be found.
source: However, when dietary sterols are not limiting, this trade-off does not need to exist and a single nutritional optimum for both lifespan and reproduction can be found.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and discussion

claim: The macronutrient balance that drives higher egg laying does not necessarily inflict a direct cost on lifespan.
source: Thus, the macronutrient balance that drives higher egg laying does not necessarily inflict a direct cost on lifespan.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and discussion

claim: Lysosomal cholesterol levels have been found to be a potent modifier of mTORC1 activity.
source: Interestingly, lysosomal cholesterol levels have recently been found to be a potent modifier of mTORC1 activity (Castellano et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: Cholesterol is an activator of TOR and cholesterol depletion inhibits its activity.
source: However, the published data shows that cholesterol is an activator of TOR and cholesterol depletion inhibits its activity.
evidence: Based on published research

claim: Long life is possible when TOR signalling is high as long as the flies have sufficient sterols in their diets.
source: These data indicate, therefore, that long life is possible when TOR signalling is high as long as the flies have sufficient sterols in their diets.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and discussion

claim: Longevity can be assured under sterol-limiting conditions by reducing the cost of reproduction, either by reducing dietary protein, by adding rapamycin which suppresses reproduction or by making flies infertile.
source: Alternatively, longevity can still be assured under sterol-limiting conditions by reducing the cost of reproduction, either by reducing dietary protein, by adding rapamycin which suppresses reproduction or by making flies infertile (Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and citation

claim: Longevity assurance in D. melanogaster is not the result of enhanced proteostasis triggered by lowered TOR, but is instead, a side effect of avoiding sterol depletion caused by an over-investment in egg production.
source: These data indicate that longevity assurance in D. melanogaster is not the result of enhanced proteostasis triggered by lowered TOR, but is instead, a side effect of avoiding sterol depletion caused by an over-investment in egg production.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and discussion

claim: Rapamycin extends the lifespan of C. elegans, yeast and mammals.
source: Rapamycin is known to extend the lifespan of various organisms including C. elegans, yeast and mammals (Harrison et al., 2009; Kapahi et al., 2010; Powers et al., 2006; Robida-Stubbs et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: C. elegans cannot synthesise its own sterols.
source: Because C. elegans cannot synthesise its own sterols, rapamycin might increase lifespan by preventing sterol depletion in a manner similar to what we have observed in Drosophila.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about C. elegans

claim: Yeast and mammals have the ability to synthesise their own sterols.
source: However, sterols may not be lifespan limiting in other organisms such as yeast and mammals that have the ability to synthesise their own sterols.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about yeast and mammalian biology

claim: Rodents will export calcium from their own bones and teeth to meet the demands of pregnancy and lactation.
source: For instance, rodents will export calcium from their own bones and teeth to meet the demands of pregnancy and lactation (Miller and Bowman, 2004; Ozbek et al., 2004; Speakman, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research

claim: All experiments were conducted using a wild type Drosophila melanogaster strain called Dahomey.
source: All experiments were conducted using a wild type Drosophila melanogaster strain called Dahomey (Mair et al., 2005).
evidence: Stated in methods section

claim: Flies were reared for two generations at a controlled density before use in experiments, to control for possible parental effects.
source: Upon removal from their population cages, flies were reared for two generations at a controlled density before use in experiments, to control for possible parental effects.
evidence: Stated in methods section

claim: Stocks were maintained and experiments were conducted at 25 °C on a 12 hr: 12 hr light:dark cycle at 65% humidity.
source: Stocks were maintained and experiments were conducted at 25 °C on a 12 hr: 12 hr light:dark cycle at 65% humidity (Bass et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated in methods section

claim: For all lifespan assays, flies were placed into vials containing 3 ml of treatment food at a density of ten flies per vial, with ten replicate vials per treatment.
source: For all lifespan assays, flies were placed into vials (﻿FS32, Pathtech) containing 3 ml of treatment food at a density of ten flies per vial, with ten replicate vials per treatment.
evidence: Stated in methods section

claim: Fecundity was measured as the sum of the mean number of eggs laid per female once per week over four weeks (commencing on approximately day 8 of the experiment).
source: Fecundity was measured as the sum of the mean number of eggs laid per female once per week over four weeks (commencing on approximately day 8 of the experiment), except for the sugar yeast (SY) medium experiment, for which egg counts were recorded in weeks one, two and three.
evidence: Stated in methods section

claim: Measuring reproductive output during the first weeks of egg laying has shown to be representative of life-long fecundity in flies.
source: ﻿These timepoints were selected because measuring reproductive output during the first weeks of egg laying has shown to be representative of life-long fecundity in flies (Chapman and Partridge, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research

claim: Cholesterol was used in the diet as opposed to ergosterol because it is easily accessible and has been shown to be adequate to support Drosophila adult nutrition to the same extend as a yeast-based diet.
source: Finally, for practical reasons we used cholesterol in the diet as opposed to ergosterol, because it is easily accessible, and where studied, has been shown to be adequate to support Drosophila adult nutrition to the same extend as a yeast-based diet (Piper et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research
